Flood insurance costs are a symptom of deeper dysfunction. H.R. 4494's 9% annual premium cap is a band-aid on FEMA's bloated National Flood Insurance Program—a $20.6B debt-ridden system that's been on GAO's high-risk list since 2006.

While Donalds targets rate spikes, the real issue is Congress' failure to modernize flood maps or incentivize private market alternatives. Since 2017, Florida's received 40% of NFIP payouts yet remains trapped in this federal monopoly.

True reform requires sunsetting FEMA's insurance role and letting states like Florida manage risk pools without DC's red tape.

The numbers don’t lie—see how federal inertia keeps Florida and other states locked into a broken system: https://t.co/w0RaIQClVZ

H.R. 4494 provides much-needed tax relief for NFIP & private insurance policyholders across SW Florida, the Sunshine State, & the nation.

Specifically, this bill combats the rising cost of flood insurance by creating a non-refundable tax deduction for flood insurance premiums. https://t.co/s1QnQlMvRX

Flood insurance costs are crushing homeowners—Donalds’ Flood Insurance Relief Act (H.R. 4494) tackles part of the problem by allowing tax deductions on premiums. But let’s be clear: this is a band-aid for systemic failure. FEMA’s National Flood Insurance Program remains bloated with bureaucratic inefficiency, outdated risk models, and endless taxpayer bailouts.

Real reform requires dismantling the NFIP’s monopoly, forcing competition from private insurers, and mandating transparency in premium calculations. Until Congress stops propping up this broken system with hidden subsidies and political favors, families will keep drowning in costs.

Accountability starts with auditing every dollar flowing through FEMA’s disaster slush funds—not just shifting the tax burden.

The Flood Insurance Relief Act offers a temporary band-aid for skyrocketing premiums but fails to address the root problem: FEMA's broken NFIP program. While a $200K income cap provides some relief, it's still taxpayer-funded subsidization of a system that's $20B in debt.

Real reform requires dismantling NFIP's bureaucratic bloat, opening flood mapping to competitive bidding, and letting private insurers truly compete without federal gatekeeping. Until then, deducting premiums just shifts costs onto other taxpayers while preserving FEMA's monopoly.

The real story is in the numbers and policy failures—see the full analysis: https://t.co/5GRFHiAgff
